Gemini said To bridge the gap between a standard image annotation viewer and an autonomous agent harness, you need to transition your tool from a human-operated canvas to a programmatic visual feedback engine.Right now, your viewer likely expects mouse events (click, drag, keystrokes). An LLM cannot reliably simulate mouse drags or guess exact pixel coordinates on a raw 1920x1080 screenshot without hallucinating and drawing boxes in random empty spaces.To make this work seamlessly in an agent harness (for instance, exposing it as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server or a structured tool-calling suite), the architecture needs to handle spatial grounding, semantic drawing commands, and collision-free layout rendering.1. The Core Bottleneck: The "Spatial Grounding" ProblemVision-Language Models (VLMs) are great at understanding what is in an image, but notoriously mediocre at predicting exact pixel coordinates [x1, y1, x2, y2] on high-resolution screenshots. If a button is at (450, 820), the model might guess (400, 750), resulting in a sloppy annotation that misses the element entirely.Three ways to solve this (and you should ideally combine them):Approach A: DOM-Assisted Grounding (Best for Live Websites)
If the agent is reviewing a live URL or a localhost build via a headless browser (like Playwright), do not make the LLM guess coordinates. Have the browser script extract the bounding boxes (getBoundingClientRect()) of interactive or structural DOM elements, assign each a unique ID, and pass that metadata alongside the screenshot. The agent simply says: "Annotate Element #14 with a red box," and your tool looks up the exact pixel coordinates of #14.Approach B: Set-of-Mark (SoM) Grid Overlay (Best for Raw Screenshots)
If the user only uploads a static PNG/JPG without DOM access, preprocess the image before sending it to the VLM. Overlay a faint coordinate grid (e.g., labeled axes every 100px, or alphanumeric grid sectors like A1, B2) or run a lightweight UI object-detection model (like OmniParser) to pre-draw numbered tags on detected UI components. The VLM reads the visual markers and references them with high accuracy.Approach C: Normalized Coordinate System (0 to 1000)
Most modern vision models are trained to output bounding boxes on a normalized scale of 0 to 1000 (where [0, 0] is top-left and [1000, 1000] is bottom-right) rather than raw pixels. Your annotation engine should accept normalized coordinates from the agent and mathematically scale them to the actual image dimensions under the hood.2. System Architecture & Workflow PipelineInstead of giving the agent low-level tools like select_brush(), move_mouse(), and type_text(), give it a declarative batch specification alongside an iterative verification loop.Ingestion & Preprocessing Layer: Takes the user's screenshot (or URL), records original dimensions, and optionally generates a "Grounding Map" (grid overlay or DOM element list) for the agent's eyes only.VLM Critique & Planning: The agent analyzes the UI/UX, identifies visual hierarchy, alignment, contrast, or spacing issues, and formulates a structured JSON payload of annotations.Smart Layout Engine (Your Canvas Tool): Takes the clean original screenshot + the agent's JSON payload. Before drawing, it calculates text wrapping, callout box placement, and arrow routing so annotations don't overlap each other or obscure the UI elements being critiqued.Self-Correction Loop (Crucial): Once your tool renders the annotations, it returns the annotated image back to the agent before showing the user. The agent inspects its own drawing: "Did my red box actually land on the submit button, or is it off by 50 pixels?" If it missed, the agent adjusts the coordinates and re-renders.3. Designing the "Doodle" Visual LanguageFor the output to look like a senior UI/UX designer reviewing a Figma board (rather than MS Paint rectangles), your annotation engine should abstract the styling into high-level semantic primitives rather than raw geometry:Primitive TypeVisual BehaviorPrimary UI/UX Use CaseHighlightBoxRounded rectangle (border-radius: 6px), dashed or solid stroke, with a 10% opacity fill of the same color.Isolating a problematic component (e.g., a broken card layout or low-contrast button).CalloutPinA numbered badge (1, 2, 3) placed on the element, connected via a curved leader line/arrow to a text label placed in the margin.Explaining complex UX issues without covering the element itself with a giant wall of text.Ruler / SpacerDouble-headed arrow (<--->) or I-beam bracket between two elements with a pixel/percentage badge in the middle.Pointing out inconsistent padding, broken grid alignments, or cramped margins.RedlineA full-width or full-height dashed guideline stretching across the viewport.Showing that two elements that should be aligned on the same axis are slightly off.FreehandDoodleSimulated SVG bezier curves with slight jitter/roughness (using a library aesthetic like Rough.js).Giving that natural "human designer sketched a circle or arrow on an iPad" feel.Spotlight / DimDarkens the entire screenshot by 50% opacity except for the bounding boxes of the highlighted areas.Focusing attention during critical hierarchy or accessibility reviews.Color Semantics (Standardized Palette)Don't let the agent pick random hex codes like #FF00FF that clash with the website. Lock the tool to semantic severity levels that auto-map to high-contrast, accessible tokens (with white outer strokes/drop-shadows so they remain visible on both dark-mode and light-mode websites):critical (Red/Coral): Broken layout, inaccessible contrast, missing primary CTA, overlapping text.warning (Amber/Orange): Inconsistent padding, weak visual hierarchy, confusing iconography.suggestion (Electric Blue/Purple): UX enhancements, micro-copy improvements, layout alternatives.positive (Emerald Green): Calling out patterns that work well and should be preserved.4. Solving the "Text Clutter" Problem (Auto-Layout Specs)If an agent tries to write a 15-word critique directly on top of a navbar, it will cover the rest of the website and become unreadable. Your existing image viewer needs an automatic layout layer for text:Dynamic Canvas Padding (The "Margin Expansion" Trick): When the agent triggers an annotation pass, automatically expand the canvas around the screenshot by adding a 250px–300px clean margin (dark or light gray) on the left, right, or bottom. The agent's boxes stay on the screenshot, while the heavy text callouts live cleanly in the outer margin with arrows pointing inward.Collision Avoidance: If two text callouts are scheduled to render within 20px of each other, your tool should apply a simple bounding-box repulsion algorithm to nudge one of the text boxes upward or downward while keeping its arrow anchored to the target coordinate.Contrast-Aware Badges: Every text box and shape drawn by the agent should automatically have a 2px contrasting outer stroke or backdrop blur so a red box is still visible on a red-themed website.5. Tool Specification for the Agent HarnessWhen you expose your image viewer to the agent harness, avoid exposing 10 separate micro-tools. Expose 2 to 3 high-level declarative tools so the agent can execute a full review in a single turn.Tool 1: inspect_ui_canvasPurpose: Prepares the image for the agent.Inputs: image_path or url, enable_grid_overlay (boolean), extract_dom_bounds (boolean).Outputs to Agent:The image (with an optional coordinate grid overlaid so the agent can read exact numbers).Image metadata (width, height, aspect_ratio).(Optional) A compact list of detected UI elements and their exact coordinates [x, y, w, h].Tool 2: render_ux_annotationsPurpose: Takes the agent's full list of visual critiques and draws them all at once onto the clean image.Inputs (Schema Specs):canvas_mode: "overlay" (draw directly on image) or "margin_callouts" (expand canvas borders for clean text placement).spotlight_mode: boolean (whether to dim un-annotated areas).annotations: An array of annotation objects. Each object contains:id: Unique identifier (e.g., "issue_1").type: "box" | "circle_doodle" | "arrow" | "ruler" | "redline".severity: "critical" | "warning" | "suggestion" | "positive".target_bounds: [x, y, width, height] (or element_id if using DOM grounding).secondary_target: [x2, y2] (used when drawing arrows or spacing rulers between two elements).label_title: Short 2–4 word header rendered directly on the tag (e.g., "Low Contrast (2.1:1)").comment: Detailed critique rendered in the callout card or sidebar legend.label_position: "auto" | "top" | "bottom" | "left" | "right" | "margin".Outputs to Agent:annotated_image_path: The newly rendered image for the agent to verify (and display to the user).layout_warnings: Any feedback from your engine (e.g., "Warning: Annotation #3 and #4 overlapped; #4 was auto-shifted 40px down.").Tool 3: update_annotationPurpose: Allows the agent (or the user in a multi-turn chat) to tweak a specific annotation without redrawing everything from scratch during the self-correction loop.Inputs: annotation_id, new_bounds, new_comment, or delete: true.6. How to Evolve Your Existing Image ViewerSince you already built a manual image viewer with annotation tools, here is the roadmap to convert it into an agent-ready harness tool:Decouple State from Mouse Events: Refactor your viewer so that every canvas drawing action is driven by a single central JSON state array (annotations = [...]). Whether a human drags a mouse or an agent sends a JSON payload, both should just push an object to this state array and trigger a canvas re-render.Add Headless Export: An agent harness often runs in a backend or CLI environment before pushing results to a UI. Ensure your viewer can take the base image + JSON state and export a flattened PNG/WebP buffer headlessly (e.g., via Node canvas, Skia, or a headless browser page).Build the "Rough / Hand-Drawn" Renderer: Standard 1px solid rectangles look robotic. Integrate a sketchy vector algorithm for arrows and circles, use pill-shaped badges for text headers, and add subtle drop shadows to callout cards.Add Interactive Bi-Directional Sync (The Killer Feature): Since you already have a viewer UI, don't just return a flat PNG to the user! Load the image and the agent's JSON layer into your interactive viewer. That way, when the agent finishes doodling its UI review, the user can click on the agent's boxes, move them around, delete ones they disagree with, or draw their own box and say back to the agent: "Look at the green box I just drew—fix the CSS for this specific container."

results.model: Gemini said To ensure a Vision-Language Model (VLM) never hallucinates coordinates or misses a UI target, the Set-of-Mark (SoM) preprocessing pipeline converts a continuous coordinate regression problem (hard for LLMs) into a discrete token classification/selection problem (what LLMs excel at).Instead of asking the agent "Where is the submit button?" and hoping it guesses [412, 850, 520, 890], you feed it an augmented image where every element and spatial region has an explicit visual anchor, while holding the exact mathematical coordinates in a lookup dictionary inside your harness.1. The Dual-Image Pipeline ArchitectureThe golden rule of an SoM pipeline is strict visual separation between what the Agent sees and what the User sees. Your tool must maintain two parallel buffers in memory:Buffer A (The Clean Source): The raw, unedited screenshot. All final UX doodles, callout boxes, and arrows will be drawn onto this buffer for the user.Buffer B (The Reference Map): A disposable clone of Buffer A, heavily tattooed with high-contrast element IDs, bounding boxes, and a coordinate grid. Only the VLM sees Buffer B.The Grounding Registry (JSON): A hidden lookup dictionary stored in the harness memory that maps every visual tag (#14, Grid_C4) to exact pixel geometry (x, y, width, height, plus computed properties like contrast and padding).2. Track 1: DOM Bounding-Box Extraction (For Live URLs / Localhost)When the agent is reviewing a website running in a headless browser, you have access to the DOM tree. However, you cannot dump every single DOM node (<div>, <span>, <li>) onto the image—a modern webpage has 1,500+ nodes, which would turn the screenshot into an unreadable wall of overlapping numbers.Phase A: Heuristic Node Filtering (Pruning the Tree)Your browser injection script must walk the DOM tree and filter down to 50–120 meaningful UI targets using four strict rules:Visibility & Viewport Check: Discard elements where display === 'none', visibility === 'hidden', opacity === 0, or where getBoundingClientRect() has a width/height less than 8px or falls outside the current viewport scroll bounds.Occlusion Culling (elementsFromPoint): A button might exist in the DOM at (200, 300), but be covered by a sticky navbar or modal. For every candidate element, run a hit-test at its center coordinate (centerX, centerY) and its four corners. If the element (or one of its direct children) is not the top-most rendered layer, discard it.Semantic & Interactive Priority: Automatically include all interactive tags (button, a, input, select, textarea, [role="button"]) and direct text-bearing leaf nodes (h1–h6, p, label, img, svg).Structural Container Deduplication (IoU Pruning): Often, a <div> wraps another <div> which wraps a <button>, all sharing the exact same bounding box. Calculate the Intersection over Union (IoU) of parent-child bounding boxes. If a parent container shares greater than 90% area overlap with its child, discard the wrapper and keep only the innermost semantic element—unless the parent container has a distinct visual boundary (a visible border, background-color different from its parent, or box-shadow).Phase B: Extracting Free UX TelemetryWhile your script is already querying the DOM for bounding boxes, extract computed CSS properties via window.getComputedStyle() and store them in the Grounding Registry alongside each ID. This gives your UX agent superpower accuracy:Exact Box Model: margin, padding, and border widths.Typography: fontSize, fontWeight, lineHeight.Color & Contrast: color and backgroundColor (allowing your harness to pre-calculate exact WCAG contrast ratios before the VLM even looks at the image).Phase C: Non-Overlapping Tag PlacementOnce you have your pruned list of [1..N] elements, render the visual markers onto Buffer B:Draw a 1.5px dashed outline around each element's exact bounding box.Attach a small, high-contrast pill badge ([12]) to the top-left outside corner of the box.Tag Collision Shifting: If Element #12 and Element #13 are tightly stacked (e.g., nav links), their top-left badges will overlap. Keep a spatial occupancy grid of placed badges; if [x, y] is already taken by another badge, slide the new badge along the top perimeter of the bounding box (top-center, top-right, or bottom-left) until it finds unoccupied space.Color-Coded Categories: Color the badges by semantic role so the VLM can parse structure at a glance—e.g., Magenta for interactive controls, Cyan for typography/text blocks, and Yellow for layout containers/cards.3. Track 2: The Coordinate Grid Fallback (For Raw Screenshots & Empty Whitespace)Even with DOM extraction, you still need a coordinate grid for two reasons:The user might upload a raw PNG (a Figma export or competitor screenshot) with no DOM available.Critiquing negative space: An agent often needs to point at empty space (e.g., "This hero section has awkward dead space on the right, add an illustration here"). Empty whitespace has no DOM node to attach a tag to.How to Design an LLM-Friendly Grid OverlayStandard pixel rulers only placed on the far top and far left edges of a 1920x1080 image fail because VLMs struggle to trace a straight imaginary line 1,200 pixels across a busy screen without drifting up or down.Instead, build a Dual-Resolution Hybrid Grid on Buffer B:Normalized 0–1000 Axis Lines: Divide the width and height into a 10 x 10 major grid (intervals of 100 on a normalized 0–1000 scale) and a 20 x 20 minor grid (intervals of 50).Adaptive Contrast Gridlines: A white grid disappears on a light-mode website; a black grid disappears on dark mode. Render gridlines using a dual-stroke technique (a 1px dark line flanked by 1px white outer glow at 25% opacity) or an invert/difference blend mode so the grid is subtly visible across any background without obscuring the UI text.In-Canvas Intersection Watermarks (The Secret Sauce): Do not just label the outer edges of the image. At every major grid intersection inside the canvas (e.g., (200, 300), (400, 600)), print a tiny, semi-transparent coordinate watermark directly at the crosshairs: 200,300. Now, no matter where the VLM looks on the screen, there is an exact numerical coordinate reference within a 50-pixel radius of its gaze.4. Track 3: Visual-Only Element Detection (When No DOM Exists)If the user uploads a static PNG/JPG without a live URL, you can still generate [#1, #2, #3] bounding boxes without a heavy machine learning setup by using a two-tier fallback:Tier 1: Classical CV Contour Detection (Zero GPU / Instant): Run the screenshot through a fast edge-detection pass (Canny edge detection + morphological dilation). UI components (buttons, inputs, cards, images) almost always have sharp rectangular boundaries or distinct background fills. Extract rectangular contours, filter out noise, and assign SoM IDs #1..#N to the detected boxes.Tier 2: Lightweight UI Detector (Optional): If you want near-DOM accuracy on static images, run a fast local ONNX pass using a specialized UI detection weights file (like OmniParser or a fine-tuned YOLOv8-UI model) combined with rapid OCR (to get exact bounding boxes of every text phrase).5. How the Agent Uses This (The Hybrid Addressing Spec)Because you have both SoM Element IDs and the In-Canvas Coordinate Grid, you can give the agent a remarkably flexible addressing system in your render_ux_annotations tool. The agent doesn't have to choose one or the other—it can mix and match them in the same tool call:Target ScenarioHow the Agent Addresses ItHow Your Harness Resolves ItCritiquing a specific component (e.g., "Make this button wider")target: { type: "element_id", id: 14 }Looks up #14 in the Grounding Registry and retrieves the exact pixel box [412, 850, 108, 40]. Zero pixel guessing.Critiquing spacing between two elements (e.g., "Too cramped between header and card")target: { type: "between_elements", id_a: 4, id_b: 9 }Calculates the shortest vertical or horizontal gap vector between the bottom edge of #4 and top edge of #9, drawing a precise <---> ruler with the exact pixel distance printed on it.Critiquing alignment across multiple items (e.g., "These three cards aren't aligned")target: { type: "element_group", ids: [18, 19, 20] }Computes either the union bounding box surrounding all three, or draws a horizontal redline across their top edges to visually expose the 4px misalignment.Pointing to empty space or un-tagged regions (e.g., "Dead whitespace here")target: { type: "grid_box", bounds: [650, 200, 900, 500] }Reads the normalized 0–1000 coordinates that the agent copied from the nearest in-canvas intersection watermark and scales them to the image's true resolution.6. End-to-End Execution Flow in the HarnessCapture: User triggers a UX review. Harness captures Buffer A (clean 1440x900 screenshot).Extract & Filter: Harness extracts DOM bounding boxes (or runs contour detection), pruning 1,200 nodes down to 65 key visual elements. Stores their exact geometry and computed CSS contrast/padding in the Grounding Registry.Stamp Buffer B: Harness clones the image into Buffer B, overlays the faint 0–1000 intersection watermarks, and draws non-overlapping numbered pills [#1] through [#65].Prompt Injection: Harness sends Buffer B to the VLM along with a compressed text summary of the Grounding Registry:"[#12] Button 'Get Started' (412x40px, contrast: 2.8:1 - FAIL) | [#13] Heading 'Pricing' (font: 24px, margin-bottom: 6px)..."Agent Output: The VLM sees both the visual tags and the hard telemetry. It outputs a structured command: "Draw a critical red highlight on #12 and a spacing ruler between #12 and #13."Clean Render: Your harness maps #12 and #13 back to their pristine pixel coordinates and draws the sketchy doodles, callouts, and arrows onto Buffer A (the clean image), returning a pixel-perfect annotated critique.
